passage: One of the best-known outcomes of broadening aesthetic experience is what we now call the aesthetics of everyday life.
Although scholarship on everyday aesthetics is flourishing today, the idea that ordinary objects and events can give aesthetic satisfaction is far from new.
Poets, especially the Romantics and many in Asian traditions, long prized the beauty of everyday situations, and novelists noticed it too.
Its modern intellectual roots, however, are most easily traced to John Dewey's Art as Experience.
There Dewey grounded aesthetic experience in the biological and cultural conditions of human life rather than treating art as something set apart.
He placed the aesthetic not in private sensation but in a full meeting of the self with the world of objects and events.
For Dewey, the aesthetic was simply the heightened, clarified form of features found in any complete experience.
